tldr: On Jun 1 Anthropic introduced Dynamic Workflows for Claude Code, a capability for tackling complex software-engineering tasks by coordinating large numbers of agents inside a single workflow. A day later Anthropic published its own account of the feature.
whats_new: Anthropic's own writeup, "A Harness For Every Task," frames Dynamic Workflows as a general orchestration harness rather than a one-off Claude Code feature.
why_it_matters: Dynamic Workflows is the orchestration primitive for fanning many agents out from a single Claude Code run — the thing to evaluate if you're moving past single-agent prompting toward parallel, structured agent pipelines.

status.detail: Dynamic Workflows is live in Claude Code, with Anthropic's own framing of how the harness works.

beats.headline: Claude Code adds Dynamic Workflows to coordinate many agents in one run
beats.summary: InfoQ reports the new capability for handling complex engineering tasks by coordinating large numbers of agents within a single workflow.

beats.headline: Anthropic frames it as "a harness for every task"
beats.summary: Anthropic's own post lays out Dynamic Workflows as a general orchestration harness for Claude Code.

open_questions: What are the concrete limits on agent count and nesting depth within one Dynamic Workflow?
How does coordinating many agents in a single workflow affect cost and latency versus sequential single-agent runs?
Does Dynamic Workflows expose hooks for deterministic control, retries, or failure handling across the fan-out?
take_for_builders: If you orchestrate agents today with bespoke glue, prototype the same fan-out as a Dynamic Workflow in Claude Code and compare cost, latency, and reliability before committing — read Anthropic's "A Harness For Every Task" for the intended model.
